The Tale of Genji. Written by Murasaki Shikibu in early eleventh-century Japan, the world's first novel—a landmark of world literature and the apex of Heian court culture. Spanning fifty-four chapters, it traces the life and romantic entanglements of Genji, son of an ancient Japanese emperor, as he navigates the aesthetic and erotic complexities of aristocratic life. The work is revolutionary for its psychological depth, interior monologue, and sustained attention to female consciousness.

Written by Murasaki Shikibu, a lady-in-waiting at the court of Emperor Ichijo, using the kana script—a Japanese phonetic writing system—rather than Chinese characters, democratizing high literature. Genji is the illegitimate son of an ancient emperor, raised in court but denied the throne; his beauty, talent, and emotional sensitivity define him more than political ambition.

The narrative spans Genji's youth through seduction and romance, his maturity through marriage, fatherhood, and political influence, to his death and the continuation of his legacy through his son and grandson. The work pioneers psychological technique: the novel enters characters' minds, shows their hidden shame and desire, and uses dream sequences, poetry, and aesthetic objects like scrolls and robes to reveal interiority.

Genji's romantic relationships are the structural spine—with multiple wives and lovers, each relationship explored with nuance and without moral judgment, unusual for the era. The work captures Heian court aesthetics: the mono no aware, the pathos of things; seasonal sensitivity; the elevation of aesthetic refinement; and Buddhist awareness of transience and sorrow.

Considered the world's first novel because of its sustained psychological realism, character development, and sophisticated narrative structure predating European novels by centuries.

Murasaki Shikibu is the author, a noble woman who wrote this masterpiece in the imperial court. The Heian period is the historical moment of this work's composition; the height of Japanese aristocratic culture. Heian culture encompasses the courtly aesthetics and values that permeate every page: beauty, poetry, seasonal awareness. Japanese literature includes this foundational work of Japanese letters; a model of indigenous literary genius. Sei Shonagon is a contemporary writer and court lady; her Pillow Book offers parallel perspective on Heian court life. The psychological novel is a precursor to modern psychological fiction; Dostoevsky and stream-of-consciousness writers saw Genji as precedent. Makura no Soshi is Sei Shonagon's contemporary essay-collection, another masterpiece of Heian women's writing.
